builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
summary: ServerBench replaces manual, expert-driven tuning of LLM serving stacks with a benchmark in which coding agents design, test, and verify complete specialized serving systems against a dollars-per-dollar objective. It costs agent API spend, GPU time for experimentation, and the added verification and stateful-replay infrastructure; only about two-thirds of runs yield verified systems. After adoption, agent-generated optimizations can introduce execution-path bugs that break correctness or session dependencies unless independently verified, and results may not transfer across workloads or deployments.
rationale: The benchmark is a research instrument rather than a production tool, and its gains depend on frontier coding agents plus serving-system verification infrastructure that a small team with one GPU cannot readily operationalize.
technique: Agentic design of LLM serving systems (ServerBench)

claims.statement: ServerBench replaces manual, expert-driven tuning of LLM serving stacks with a benchmark in which coding agents design, test, and verify complete specialized serving systems against a dollars-per-dollar objective. It costs agent API spend, GPU time for experimentation, and the added verification and stateful-replay infrastructure; only about two-thirds of runs yield verified systems. After adoption, agent-generated optimizations can introduce execution-path bugs that break correctness or session dependencies unless independently verified, and results may not transfer across workloads or deployments.
Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, 4.87x the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs produce verified systems and 13 exceed the strongest baseline.
